title: 'It's Real Now': With Law Firm AI Use on the Rise, Expect Alternative Fee Arrangements to Pick Up Steam in 2026
author: Jon Campisi

st.t: Firm resilience: High profits may conceal structural weakness
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s profitability paradox: conventional demand and rate increases can sustain strong financial results even as AI efficiency increases client scrutiny of hourly billing and value. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution that the eventual effects on client–firm relationships and work allocation remain uncertain.
qs: Demand growth, billing rate increases, and investing in associate hiring helped Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath achieve double-digit increases across all financial metrics in 2025.

kp.k: Alternative fee arrangements may gain momentum in 2026
kp.d: The article predicts that 2026 may mark greater legal-industry openness to alternative fee arrangements after decades of discussion about ending the billable hour. This is a forward-looking claim rather than a documented finding; the subscription-limited text provides no supporting data, examples, or methodology.
qs: While the death of the billable hour has been discussed for years, 2026 may finally be the year where the legal industry becomes more open to alternative billing arrangements.

kp.k: AI efficiencies may weaken hourly billing’s appeal
kp.d: The article identifies efficiencies from applying artificial intelligence to client matters as a likely driver of movement from hourly billing toward alternative fee arrangements. It does not quantify those efficiencies or specify the technologies, legal tasks, practice areas, firms, or clients involved.
qs: The push toward AFAs over hourly billing is likely due to the efficiencies created by artificial intelligence used in client matters.

kp.k: Client frustration may accelerate pricing-model change
kp.d: The article links dissatisfaction with rising legal rates and increased use of technology in legal work to a possible acceleration away from the billable hour. The available text frames this as a possibility and supplies no direct client evidence or measured market trend.
qs: But client frustration with rising rates and the growing application of technology to legal work may finally start accelerating the transition.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Campisi predicts that growing law-firm AI use will help accelerate interest in alternative fee arrangements in 2026.
pts.d: The accessible headline, introduction and summary frame AI-created efficiencies in client matters, together with client frustration over rising rates, as drivers of a potential transition away from hourly billing. The prediction is increased openness to alternative fee arrangements, not a definite end to the billable hour. No interviewed speaker is identified in the accessible article text, so the claim is attributed to Campisi's reporting rather than to an inferred speaker behind the headline quotation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The accessible excerpt offers a causal explanation but no supporting empirical evidence or named expert testimony.
pts.d: AI efficiencies and client frustration with rising rates are asserted as reasons to expect billing changes. No adoption figures, efficiency measurements, billing data, case studies or named interviewees appear in the supplied article excerpt. The subscription barrier prevents assessing what evidence the full article supplies. The later 'Continue Reading' teasers concern separate articles and are not evidence presented for Campisi's forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Published December 18, 2025, the article forecasts possible acceleration in 2026, using explicitly qualified language.
pts.d: The source contrasts decades of discussion about the billable hour's demise with a prospective change in 2026. Its wording—'may finally' and 'likely'—qualifies both the forecast and its proposed cause. The implied conditions are growing use of AI in client work, resulting efficiencies and continued client frustration with rising rates. It does not specify an adoption threshold or a deadline for replacing hourly billing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The forecast concerns law firms' billing arrangements and the clients paying for AI-assisted legal work.
pts.d: Law firms are portrayed as increasingly applying AI to client matters and potentially becoming more open to alternatives to hourly billing. Clients are described as frustrated by rising rates, contributing to pressure for that transition. The excerpt does not distinguish firm size, practice area or client segment, or quantify effects on fees, profitability, employment or access to justice.
